all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: prototype
concepts.definition: A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that can be built quickly to model or demonstrate a design idea and to test whether it will work in practice. It can be discarded after testing or refined into the final product.

defining_facts.text: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

Quick evaluation of design ideas in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle requires both a prototype that models or demonstrates the design idea and can be built quickly, and a quick evaluation method for testing the prototype; both requirements are equally important for a quick execution of the cycle.
Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first.

A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or, in the best case, it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

concepts.name: user feedback
concepts.definition: User feedback is the involvement of users in different ways, not only through feedback, that iterations between stages in an interactive system development lifecycle account for.

defining_facts.text: In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

concepts.name: code testing
concepts.definition: Code testing is a standard software development stage in interactive system development that evaluates code as part of coding and implementation by ensuring it is bug-free and executes properly, but does not establish whether the system is usable.

defining_facts.text: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

In the coding stage, code testing can reveal issues that require returning to code design, creating an iteration; fewer iterations are preferred because code design is a highly skilled, costly process and late problems are costly to rewrite and test.

The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.
Code testing tests the executability of code by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view.

The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.

concepts.name: empirical study
concepts.definition: Empirical study is a usability-testing stage in interactive system development, performed after code testing, that systematically tests a fully implemented system with end users through a controlled experiment to collect and analyze data for assessing overall usability.

defining_facts.text: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.
The empirical study stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development and is typically not part of other software development in which end users are not involved.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, usability study, or empirical research, is a stage in interactive system development in which the usability of a developed system is evaluated with end users.
In interactive system development, empirical evaluation follows the code testing stage, which produces an executable system but does not establish that the system is usable.

A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

A controlled experiment used for usability evaluation is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, or a user study, and in the context of usability evaluation it can also be called a usability study.

An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

An empirical study, after a system has been fully implemented, is the process of setting up an experiment, executing the experiment, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure the usability of the implemented interface.

The first stage in an empirical study is formulating a research question, and the experiment is conducted to find the answer to that question, with observations or empirical data collection and data analysis performed based on the question.
Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, empirical research, or usability research, means observation in the real world of real users.
Empirical evaluation is carried out at the end, when the system is fully implemented, to obtain an idea of the overall usability of the system.
The empirical research process has four stages, the first stage being research question framing and the second stage being variables.

In empirical research, research question framing addresses broader generalizable questions that are untestable by framing multiple testable research questions, collecting objective data for each, reaching a definite conclusion for each, and combining those conclusions to draw a conclusion about the untestable questions.

In the variables stage of empirical research, the variables in the testable questions are identified to design an experiment; the two most important variable types are independent variables, or factors, which can take levels or values, and dependent variables, which depend on the factors and levels.

concepts.name: interactive system development lifecycle
concepts.definition: Interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC) is a staged development method that is similar to regular software development but distinctive in its end-user requirement gathering, iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical usability evaluation.

defining_facts.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

The book Human-Computer Interaction, User-Centric Computing for Design discusses the stages of interactive system development life cycles in more detail with respect to broader interactive system development concerns.

The final design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was developed using the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDL) model, an iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle that started with a design based on design guidelines and continuously refined design ideas from feedback and observations obtained by involving end users passively or actively.
In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.
The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality (XR) systems.

The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

In the interactive system development lifecycle, cycles should generally be kept infrequent because frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent.

never_defined.name: graphical user interface
never_defined.definition: Graphical user interface (GUI) is a drag-and-drop interface that most standalone augmented reality authoring tools provide to allow users with basic personal computer skills to create applications without coding.

never_defined.name: interface
never_defined.definition: An interface is the way a system interfaces with users, its environment, and other systems, letting users provide input, see outcomes, and act on outcomes; on a computer screen it is the whole content seen there.

never_defined.name: system
never_defined.definition: A system is a developed, executable thing whose usability is evaluated with end users in interactive system development.

never_defined.name: usability issue
never_defined.definition: Usability issue is a problem in the usability of an interface or prototype that evaluators identify during evaluations, and that users are likely to face while performing tasks.

never_defined.name: fully implemented system
never_defined.definition: Fully implemented system is the overall system, rather than a prototype, that is evaluated in a conclusive usability assessment.

never_defined.name: user behavioral data
never_defined.definition: User behavioral data is data that a controlled experiment collects and analyzes for a conclusive usability assessment of a fully implemented system.

never_defined.name: research question
never_defined.definition: A research question is a question formulated in the first stage of an empirical study, which the experiment is conducted to answer and on which data collection and analysis are based, and it should avoid generalized concepts that make it untestable.

never_defined.name: variable
never_defined.definition: A variable is an item in a testable research question that is identified after the research questions are formulated, without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed; its two most important types are independent variables, or factors, that can take levels or values, and dependent variables that depend on those factors and levels.

never_defined.name: data
never_defined.definition: Data are collected in an experiment and analyzed to reach a reliable conclusion about a system's overall usability aspects.

never_defined.name: empirical data
never_defined.definition: Empirical data is data collected in an experiment or empirical study that answers a research question, and it is processed and tested for statistical significance before conclusions are drawn.

never_defined.name: text entry
never_defined.definition: Text entry is a graphical user interface whose quality can be judged by users.

never_defined.name: text input interface
never_defined.definition: A text input interface is an interface that lets a user enter text.

never_defined.name: Microsoft Word
never_defined.definition: Microsoft Word (MS Word) is a text input interface compared with a new text input interface on quality and speed.

never_defined.name: standalone evaluation
never_defined.definition: Standalone evaluation is an evaluation that elicits feedback.

never_defined.name: text input task
never_defined.definition: A Text input task is a task in which a user enters text, used to compare interfaces on speed.

never_defined.name: subjective interpretation
never_defined.definition: Subjective interpretation is a user's interpretation that non-testable research questions depend on, while testable research questions allow objective conclusions to be drawn independently of it.

never_defined.name: text entry speed
never_defined.definition: Text entry speed is objective data that is logged as characters per minute (CPM) and used to determine which text entry interface is faster.

never_defined.name: subjective feedback
never_defined.definition: Subjective feedback is feedback that is problematic to depend on, as responses can split and may not support a definitive conclusion.

never_defined.name: objective data
never_defined.definition: Objective data is data, such as text entry speed or task performance data, that can be collected and analyzed to draw objective conclusions independently of users' subjective interpretation.

never_defined.name: scientific conclusion
never_defined.definition: A scientific conclusion is a reliable, definite conclusion that testable research questions allow, because they support objective data collection rather than subjective user feedback.

never_defined.name: generalized concept
never_defined.definition: A generalized concept is a concept, such as whether something is good, that is ambiguous and can lead to untestable research questions.

never_defined.name: testability
never_defined.definition: Testability is one side of a trade-off with generalization in empirical study, balanced by framing testable research questions covering different aspects of a system.

never_defined.name: generalization
never_defined.definition: Generalization is the empirical-study aim of reaching a definitive conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question by combining conclusions from multiple testable research questions covering different aspects of a system.

never_defined.name: text entry rate
never_defined.definition: Text entry rate (TER) is a dependent variable in research question 3 (RQ3), whose value depends on the levels of the interface.
